intro.carita: Uttama Carita (the third episode, chapters 5–13), of which this is the first of the two battles with the asura brothers. In the recitation tradition its presiding form is Mahāsarasvatī; this is the Gita Press viniyoga (printed before chapter 5), not a statement of the Purāṇa text. In the Gita Press pāṭha chapter 9 has no viniyoga of its own, only a dhyāna, and it pictures not the Goddess alone but Ardhanārīśvara: the body that is half Ambikā and half Īśa (अर्धाम्बिकेशम्), shining like the bandhūka flower and like gold, holding in its arms a fine rosary, the noose and the goad, and granting boons, adorned with the crescent moon, three-eyed. The dhyāna is liturgy; the chapter itself never mentions Śiva’s half-female form.
intro.summary: King Suratha calls the slaying of Raktabīja wonderful and asks what Śumbha and the furious Niśumbha did next (9.1–3). Medhas answers: both brothers flew into a rage (9.4–5). Niśumbha charged with the pick of the asura army, his champions guarding him on every side, and Śumbha, who had been fighting the Mothers, came on too (9.6–8). The brothers rained arrows on the Devī like two storm-clouds; Caṇḍikā cut them down and wounded both (9.9–10). Niśumbha struck her lion on the head, and one after another his weapons were destroyed — sword and shield by a razor-headed arrow, his śakti by her discus, his spear by her fist, his mace burnt to ash by her trident — until, coming on axe in hand, he was felled by her arrows (9.11–16). Śumbha took his place, eight-armed in his chariot, filling the sky (9.17–18). The Goddess answered with sound: her conch and bowstring, her bell that drains the Daityas’ tejas, the lion’s roar, Kālī striking sky and earth so that every earlier sound was drowned, and Śivadūtī’s laughter, at which the asuras trembled (9.19–23). She cried ‘Stand, wicked one, stand!’ and the gods in the sky cried ‘Victory!’ (9.24). Śumbha’s flaming dart was struck aside by a great firebrand, his roar was overcome by a crash like thunder, and the two cut each other’s arrows by the thousand (9.25–27), until Caṇḍikā struck him with her spear and he fell senseless (9.28). Niśumbha, recovering, shot at the Goddess, Kālī and the lion, made himself ten thousand arms and buried Caṇḍikā under discuses; Durgā cut them all down (9.29–31). He charged with a mace, which she cut through with her sword before it reached her; he took up a spear, and she pierced his heart with hers (9.32–34). From his heart came another being, mighty and crying ‘Stop!’; laughing aloud, the Goddess struck off its head, and he fell (9.35–36). The lion, Kālī and Śivadūtī devoured the asuras, and the Mothers — Kaumārī, Brahmāṇī, Māheśvarī, Vārāhī, Vaiṣṇavī and Aindrī — destroyed the rest with their own weapons; some perished, some fled (9.37–41).
intro.forms: The Devī (9.2, 9.7, 9.9 and throughout the duels); Caṇḍikā, ‘the fierce one’, the name the battle verses use most (9.8, 9.10, 9.15, 9.28, 9.30, 9.32–34); Ambikā, ‘Mother’, even in battle (9.17, 9.24); Bhagavatī Durgā, ‘who destroys distress in hard places’ (दुर्गार्तिनाशिनी, 9.31). Beside her fight her own powers: Kālī, who struck sky and earth (9.22, 9.29, 9.37, 9.41); Śivadūtī, whose laughter shook the asuras (9.23, 9.37, 9.41); and the Mothers (मातृ, 9.8) named with their weapons — Kaumārī and Brahmāṇī (9.38), Māheśvarī and Vārāhī (9.39), Vaiṣṇavī and Aindrī (9.40); Nārasiṃhī is not named here. Her lion fights throughout (9.11, 9.21, 9.29, 9.37, 9.41).
intro.significance: The chapter is named for the first of the two brothers to die (colophon: निशुम्भवधः). It is built as a series of answers: every weapon Niśumbha takes up is destroyed by a different weapon of hers (9.11–16, 9.31–33), and Śumbha’s show of eight arms is answered by sound before any blow (9.18–23). The Goddess still fights with her companions — Kālī, Śivadūtī, the lion and the Mothers — and the rout at the end is theirs as much as hers (9.37–41). That sets up chapter 10, where Śumbha, the brother kept alive by a swoon (9.28), taunts her for fighting by the strength of others (10.3), and she draws them all back into herself (10.5–6).
intro.grammar: A battle narrative in the perfect: reduplicated forms (चिच्छेद, चिक्षेप, जग्राह, विव्याध, अभिजघान), the weak perfects with e and no reduplication (त्रेसुः, 9.23; नेशुः, 9.38; पेतुः, 9.39; विनेशुः, 9.41), and the periphrastic perfect of causative stems (ताडयामास, 9.10; पूरयामास, 9.20–21; छादयामास, 9.30). Locative absolutes set each new turn (रक्तबीजे निपातिते, 9.3, 9.5; ताडिते वाहने, 9.12; छिन्ने चर्मणि खड्गे च, 9.13; the long one of 9.17). Past participles often stand as the finite verb (आगता, 9.15; निरस्ता, 9.25; निःसृतः, 9.35), and 9.26 has the past active participle in -तवत् (जितवान्). The learner also meets an impersonal passive of speech (जयेत्यभिहितं देवैः, 9.24), causatives in both padas (अपातयत, 9.16; अभ्यधावत beside अभ्यधावत्, 9.32, 9.6), samprasāraṇa in √व्यध् (आविध्य, 9.15; विव्याध, आविद्ध, 9.34), the distributive -शस् (शतशः, सहस्रशः, 9.27), the च्वि construction (चूर्णीकृताः, 9.39) and repetition for distribution (खण्डं खण्डम्, 9.40).
intro.teaching: Literally, Niśumbha attacks, is felled, recovers and is killed; Śumbha is struck senseless; the asura army is devoured, slain or scattered. As teaching, the Śākta tradition reads the chapter for what it shows of the Goddess: nothing aimed at her reaches her (each weapon is undone, 9.11–16, 9.25, 9.31–33); her presence alone, as sound, drains the enemy’s strength before the fight (9.20, 9.23); and the Mothers, Kālī and Śivadūtī are her own powers acting as many (9.37–41). The figure that leaves Niśumbha’s pierced heart still crying ‘Stop!’ (9.35–36) is not explained by the text; reading it as the force that drove him, which must be cut down where it emerges, is interpretation, and is offered as such in the commentary.

conclusion.narrative: Suratha asks what the asura brothers did after Raktabīja’s death, and Medhas tells of their last army and their duels with the Goddess. Niśumbha loses weapon after weapon and falls; Śumbha, towering in his chariot, is answered by the sounds of the Goddess and her companions, matches her arrows for a moment, and is struck senseless. Niśumbha rises, multiplies his arms, charges again and is pierced through the heart; a second figure comes out of him crying ‘Stop!’ and is beheaded by the laughing Goddess. Her lion, Kālī, Śivadūtī and the Mothers destroy or scatter the rest. The chapter ends with Śumbha still alive, lying stunned (9.28), for the last battle of chapter 10.

constructions: Locative absolutes marking each turn of the battle (रक्तबीजे निपातिते, 9.3, 9.5; ताडिते वाहने, 9.12; तस्मिन् निपतिते भूमौ निशुम्भे … भ्रातरि, 9.17).
The weak perfect with e and no reduplication (त्रेसुः, 9.23; नेशुः, 9.38; पेतुः, 9.39; विनेशुः, 9.41) beside reduplicated perfects (चिच्छेद, विव्याध, अभिजघान).
The periphrastic perfect of causative and curādi stems (ताडयामास, 9.10; पूरयामास, 9.20–21; छादयामास, 9.30).
Participles as the main verb: the past participle of motion (आगता, 9.15; निःसृतः, 9.35), the passive participle (निरस्ता, 9.25) and the past active participle in -तवत् (जितवान्, 9.26).
An impersonal passive of speech with its agent in the instrumental, in a यदा … तदा frame (जयेत्यभिहितं देवैः, 9.24).
One singular verb serving two or three subjects (चकार, 9.3, 9.5; चिच्छेद, 9.27; चखाद, 9.37).
The च्वि construction (चूर्णीकृताः, 9.39) and āmreḍita repetition for distribution (खण्डं खण्डं कृताः, 9.40).
Bahuvrīhis of the weapon in hand (परशुहस्तम्, 9.16; आत्तकार्मुकः, 9.29; शूलहस्तम्, 9.34).
insights: Nothing aimed at the Goddess reaches her: each of Niśumbha’s weapons is undone by a different one of hers, and once by her fist alone (9.11–16, 9.31–33).

Her power acts as sound before it acts as a blow: the bell destroys the tejas of the Daitya hosts (9.20), Kālī’s blow drowns every other sound (9.22), and at Śivadūtī’s laughter the asuras tremble (9.23).

Kālī, Śivadūtī and the Mothers are her own powers fighting as many; each Mother wields her god’s weapon, so the gods’ powers win as forms of the Goddess (8.13, 9.38–40), and in 10.5–6 she draws them back into herself.
Durgā is named here by what she does: she destroys the distress of those in hard straits (दुर्गार्तिनाशिनी, 9.31).
The gods do not fight in this carita; their part is to cry ‘Victory!’ from the sky as she challenges the asura (9.24), as later they will praise her in chapter 11.

The asura’s force is not ended by the first wound: something comes out of Niśumbha’s pierced heart still defiant, and only when it is cut down does he fall (9.35–36); the text leaves the figure unexplained.
conclusion.srividya: The chapter shares names with the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa): Caṇḍikā (755, चण्डिका), Ambikā (295, अम्बिका), Durgā (190, दुर्गा) — followed there by दुःखहन्त्री (191), much as 9.31 glosses Durgā as दुर्गार्तिनाशिनी — and Śivadūtī (405, शिवदूती), a name whose origin the Devī Māhātmya itself tells (8.23–28) and which the Lalitā Sahasranāma lists as a name. The battle images have parallels in the Lalitā Sahasranāma’s war with Bhaṇḍāsura: the Goddess answering the asura’s weapons with her own (79, भण्डासुरेन्द्रनिर्मुक्तशस्त्रप्रत्यस्त्रवर्षिणी; compare 9.10–16, 9.27) and accompanied by an army of śaktis (65, भण्डासुरवधोद्युक्तशक्तिसेनासमन्विता; compare the Mothers, 9.38–40). The stories are different, and these are shared Śākta names and images, not evidence that one text depends on the other; no specifically Śrīvidyā doctrine is stated in this chapter.

key_verses.why: She fills the quarters with the sound of her bell, which destroys the tejas of all the Daitya hosts.
Kālī leaps up and strikes sky and earth with both hands, and every earlier sound is drowned in the din.
Ambikā cries ‘Stand, wicked one, stand!’, and the gods in the sky cry ‘Victory!’
Bhagavatī Durgā, destroyer of distress in hard straits, cuts down Niśumbha’s discuses and arrows.
From Niśumbha’s pierced heart comes another being, mighty and valiant, crying ‘Stop!’
Laughing aloud, the Goddess cuts off its head with her sword, and he falls: the slaying that names the chapter.
The Mothers join the rout: Kaumārī’s spear and the water hallowed by Brahmāṇī’s mantras destroy the asuras.

sandhi_patterns: Visarga sandhi is the commonest junction: -aḥ before voiced sounds → -o (शुम्भो यत्कर्म, ततो युद्धम्), visarga → ś/s before c/t (निशुम्भश्च, शिरश्चिच्छेद, पेतुस्तथापरे), and -aḥ + a → -o’ (निशुम्भोऽथ, 9.6; सोऽसुरः, 9.13; शतशोऽथ, 9.27; ततोऽसावपतद्भुवि, 9.36).
सः drops its visarga before consonants (स रथस्थः, 9.18; स तदाभिहतो, 9.28; स च, 9.33).

Final n before ś, t and c: n + ś → ñch (चिच्छेदास्ताञ्छरान्, 9.10; शुम्भमुक्ताञ्छरान्, 9.27); n → ṃs before t (शरांस्ताभ्याम्, 9.10; दुरात्मंस्तिष्ठ, 9.24; असुरांस्तान्, 9.37); n → ṃś before c (सायकांश्च, 9.31).

Final t assimilates: before a nasal → n (अभ्यधावन्निशुम्भो, 9.6; केचिन्नेशुः, 9.38; हृदयान्निःसृतः, 9.35), before c → c (केचिच्चूर्णीकृताः, 9.39), voiced before a voiced sound (केचिद्विनेशुः, 9.41; अपतद्भुवि, 9.36).

Vowel sandhi of every kind across words and in compounds: savarṇa-dīrgha (चादाय, शूलेनाभिजघान), guṇa (तिष्ठेति, महोल्कया), yaṇ (हतेष्वन्येषु, भ्रातर्यतीव), vṛddhi (संदष्टौष्ठपुटाः, 9.7; चैन्द्री-, 9.40).
No declared hiatus in the chapter.
samasa: Bahuvrīhis of the weapon in hand and of epithet (परशुहस्तम्, शूलहस्तम्, आत्तकार्मुकः; महावीर्यः, महाबलः, भीमविक्रमे, शितधारेण, अष्टचन्द्रकम्).

Tṛtīyā tatpuruṣas built on ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣas for the Mothers and their weapons (कौमारीशक्तिनिर्भिन्नाः, ब्रह्माणीमन्त्रपूतेन, 9.38; माहेश्वरीत्रिशूलेन, वाराहीतुण्डघातेन, 9.39; ऐन्द्रीहस्ताग्रविमुक्तेन, a pañcamī tatpuruṣa, 9.40).
Upapada tatpuruṣas with agent forms (दुर्गार्तिनाशिनी, 9.31; तेजोवधविधायिना, 9.20; अमरार्दनम्, 9.34; दितिजः, दनुजेश्वरः, 9.30; रथस्थः, 9.18).

Upamāna-pūrvapada karmadhārayas of sound (सिंहनादेन, निर्घातनिःस्वनः, 9.26), itaretara dvandvas (शुम्भनिशुम्भयोः, 9.9; कालीशिवदूतीमृगाधिपैः, 9.41), a gati compound (चूर्णीकृताः, 9.39), and nested bahuvrīhis (त्याजितेभमहामदैः, 9.21; दंष्ट्राक्षुण्णशिरोधरान्, 9.37).
grammar_notes: Weak perfects with e and no reduplication are taken as regular for their roots: त्रेसुः (9.23), नेशुः (9.38), पेतुः (9.39), विनेशुः (9.41).
√धाव् appears in both padas: parasmaipada अभ्यधावत् (9.6) and ātmanepada अभ्यधावत (9.32); the causative अपातयत (9.16) is ātmanepada too.
निर्घातनिःस्वनो … जितवान् (9.26) has no expressed object or source; the reading ‘overcame Śumbha’s roar’ follows the context, as does supplying the Goddess as the agent of निरस्ता (9.25).
Several sentences carry an unstated subject over from the previous verse (the Devī in 9.13 and 9.20; Śumbha in 9.17–18, where the verse names him only as the brother).
वैष्णव्या (9.40) is divided as the instrumental; the genitive वैष्णव्याः gives the same printed text.
In 9.9 शरवर्षम् is taken as the object of वर्षतोः; it can also stand in apposition to युद्धम्.
themes: The Mothers, Kālī and Śivadūtī as her powers
The death of Niśumbha; Śumbha kept for chapter 10
uncertain: No variant readings are recorded for this chapter in corrections.json; the Gita Press text is followed as printed.

Interpretive doubts, none about the reading itself, are flagged on 9.9 (construction of शरवर्षम्), 9.11 (whether सुप्रभम् qualifies the shield or the sword), 9.18 (construal of अत्युच्चैः), 9.22 (गगनम् as object or goal), 9.25 (the unexpressed agent of निरस्ता; what महोल्का is), 9.26 (the source of the thunderclap and the object of जितवान्), 9.35 (the identity of the अपरः पुरुषः), 9.36 (the referent of असौ) and 9.40 (वैष्णव्या or वैष्णव्याः in the padaccheda).

comm.t: Suratha sums up chapter 8 — the Devī and the Mothers against Raktabīja, whose every drop of blood became a new asura until Kālī drank it — and calls it विचित्र, ‘marvellous’.

The question keeps the frame of the text alive: the third (uttama) carita, like the first two, is told as Medhas’s answer to the king. The Gita Press pāṭha assigns this carita to Mahāsarasvatī as its presiding form; that is liturgical tradition, not a statement of the verse.

mantras.anvaya: रक्तबीजे निपातिते शुम्भः अतिकोपनः निशुम्भः च यत् कर्म चकार, (तत्) अहं भूयः च श्रोतुम् इच्छामि।
mantras.anvaya_en: The main clause (अहं … श्रोतुम् इच्छामि) takes as its object a relative clause (यत् कर्म चकार …); the correlative तत् is supplied. रक्तबीजे निपातिते is a locative absolute giving the time.
mantras.lit: And further I wish to hear what deed Śumbha did, and the exceedingly wrathful Niśumbha, when Raktabīja had been felled.
mantras.tr: I wish to hear more: once Raktabīja had been struck down, what did Śumbha do, and Niśumbha in his towering rage?
mantras.tr_note: The relative clause is turned into a question for natural English.

comm.t: Suratha asks for the sequel: the deeds of the two brothers, Śumbha and Niśumbha, the lords of the asuras whose generals have now all fallen. Chapter 9 answers for Niśumbha; chapter 10 for Śumbha.

A modern reading: the king asks to hear ‘more’ (भूयः). In this text listening is not idle — the whole Māhātmya is offered as something heard, and the hearing itself is what transforms Suratha and Samādhi.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two locative absolutes (रक्तबीजे निपातिते; अन्येषु हतेषु) set the scene; the main clause is शुम्भासुरः निशुम्भः च … कोपं चकार.
mantras.lit: Raktabīja having been felled, and the others having been slain in battle, the asura Śumbha and Niśumbha made immeasurable anger.
mantras.tr: With Raktabīja struck down and the others slain in battle, the asura Śumbha and Niśumbha flew into a rage beyond all measure.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Made anger’ (कोपं चकार) is rendered idiomatically as ‘flew into a rage’.

comm.t: Medhas answers the king’s question at once: the loss of Raktabīja and the rest of the army drives both brothers to fury. The asura commanders of the uttama carita — Dhūmralocana, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, Raktabīja — have now all fallen; only the two lords remain.
A modern reading: the text repeatedly shows anger rising as defeat closes in. The rage of the brothers is not strength but the last form their pride takes.

mantras.lit: Seeing the great army being slain, bearing indignation, Niśumbha then rushed forward with the chief asura army.
mantras.tr: Seeing his great army being cut down, Niśumbha, seething with fury, charged forward with the pick of the asura host.

comm.t: Niśumbha, the younger brother, takes the field first, with the best of the remaining troops. अमर्ष is the anger of one who cannot bear an affront or a defeat.
Chapter 9 is named for him (निशुम्भवधः): his charge here opens the battle that ends with his death (9.34–36).

mantras.lit: In front of him, and likewise behind, and on both sides, great asuras, biting their lips, enraged, came up to kill the Devī.
mantras.tr: Before him, behind him and on either flank the great asuras advanced, biting their lips in rage, bent on killing the Goddess.

comm.t: Niśumbha’s champions form a guard on every side of him as they close on the Devī. Biting the lips is the epic sign of fury.

mantras.anvaya: महावीर्यः शुम्भः अपि मातृभिः तु युद्धं कृत्वा स्वबलैः वृतः कोपात् चण्डिकां निहन्तुम् आजगाम।

mantras.lit: Śumbha too, of great valour, surrounded by his own forces, came to slay Caṇḍikā out of anger, having done battle with the Mothers.
mantras.tr: Mighty Śumbha too came on, ringed by his own troops, to slay Caṇḍikā in his wrath, after doing battle with the Mothers.

comm.t: The elder brother joins the attack. The Mothers (मातृ) are the śaktis of the gods who joined the Devī in chapter 8 (Brahmāṇī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, Aindrī); Śumbha has been fighting them, and now turns on Caṇḍikā herself.
The Mothers remain on the field through this chapter; at its end (9.38–40) they are named again as they destroy the remaining asuras.

mantras.anvaya: ततः देव्या शुम्भनिशुम्भयोः (च) अतीव युद्धम् आसीत्, (तयोः) मेघयोः इव अतीव उग्रं शरवर्षं वर्षतोः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The main clause is युद्धम् आसीत्; the participle वर्षतोः, agreeing with शुम्भनिशुम्भयोः, takes शरवर्षम् as its object, and मेघयोः इव is the simile. Alternatively शरवर्षम् is nominative in apposition to युद्धम् (‘a most fierce rain of arrows, as of two clouds raining’); the sense is the same.
mantras.lit: Then there was an exceedingly (fierce) battle of the Devī with Śumbha and Niśumbha, (the two) raining an exceedingly fierce shower of arrows, like two clouds raining.
mantras.tr: Then a furious battle broke out between the Goddess and Śumbha and Niśumbha, who poured on her a terrible shower of arrows, like two storm-clouds pouring rain.
mantras.tr_note: ‘On her’ and ‘storm-’ make the simile explicit in English; the Sanskrit has only ‘like two clouds raining’.

comm.t: Both brothers now fight the Devī together. The simile of the two rain-clouds pictures the volleys of arrows falling as thick as monsoon rain.

flags.uncertain: Construction of शरवर्षम्: object of वर्षतोः (taken here) or nominative in apposition to युद्धम्. Both are grammatical and give the same picture.

mantras.lit: Caṇḍikā cut the arrows shot by those two with masses of her own arrows, and struck the two lords of the asuras on their limbs with floods of weapons.
mantras.tr: Caṇḍikā cut down the arrows the two of them shot with volleys of her own, and struck the two asura lords all over their bodies with a torrent of weapons.

comm.t: The Devī answers both brothers at once: she destroys their arrows in flight and then wounds them both. The duals (ताभ्याम्, असुरेश्वरौ) keep the two brothers fighting side by side.
Caṇḍikā, ‘the fierce one’, is the name the Devī Māhātmya uses most for her in battle. Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same name (755, चण्डिका); the two works remain distinct.

mantras.anvaya_en: The absolutive phrase (… आदाय) precedes the main verb अताडयत्; सिंहम् is its object, with वाहनम् उत्तमम् in apposition, and मूर्ध्नि gives the place struck.
mantras.lit: Niśumbha, taking a sharpened sword and a gleaming shield, struck the lion, the Devī’s excellent mount, on the head.
mantras.tr: Niśumbha took up a keen sword and a gleaming shield and struck the lion, the Goddess’s noble mount, on the head.

comm.t: Niśumbha changes weapons and attacks not the Devī but her lion. The lion fights throughout the uttama carita and returns in 9.21 and 9.37.

flags.uncertain: सुप्रभम् may qualify चर्म (n.) or खड्गम् (m.); the accusative singular form is the same. Its place after चर्म च आदाय favours the shield.

mantras.anvaya_en: A locative absolute (ताडिते वाहने) sets the time; one main verb चिच्छेद governs two objects (असिम् and चर्म), both owned by निशुम्भस्य.
mantras.lit: The mount having been struck, the Devī with a razor-headed arrow swiftly cut Niśumbha’s excellent sword, and also his shield with eight moons.
mantras.tr: When her mount was struck, the Goddess swiftly cut through Niśumbha’s fine sword with a razor-headed arrow, and his shield emblazoned with eight moons as well.

comm.t: The Devī answers the blow to her lion by disarming Niśumbha: one arrow, sword and shield both cut. The ‘eight-mooned’ shield is a conventional epic description of a richly ornamented shield. From 9.11 to 9.16 the scene is a sequence: each weapon Niśumbha takes up — sword and shield, śakti, spear, mace, axe — is destroyed by a different weapon of the Devī.

mantras.anvaya: चर्मणि खड्गे च छिन्ने सः असुरः शक्तिं चिक्षेप; (देवी) अस्य अभिमुखागतां ताम् अपि चक्रेण द्विधा चक्रे।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences. The first: locative absolute (छिन्ने …), then सः असुरः शक्तिं चिक्षेप. The second has the Devī as its unstated subject: ताम् … द्विधा चक्रे.
mantras.lit: Shield and sword having been cut, that asura hurled a śakti; that too of his, coming face-on, (she) made into two with her discus.
mantras.tr: With his shield and sword cut down, the asura hurled a śakti; and as it flew straight at her, she split it in two with her discus.

comm.t: Niśumbha’s third weapon, the śakti (a heavy throwing spear), is met by the Devī’s discus. The subject of चक्रे, the Devī, is understood from the previous verse.
A modern reading: the narrative is built as a sequence of escalations each answered completely. Nothing the asura takes up survives contact with her.

mantras.anvaya: अथ कोपाध्मातः दानवः निशुम्भः शूलं जग्राह; आयातं तत् च अपि देवी मुष्टिपातेन अचूर्णयत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: Niśumbha’s action (शूलं जग्राह) and the Devī’s (तत् … अचूर्णयत्), joined by च.
mantras.lit: Then Niśumbha the Dānava, swollen with anger, seized a spear; and that too, as it came, the Devī crushed to powder with a blow of her fist.
mantras.tr: Then Niśumbha the Dānava, bursting with rage, seized a spear; and as it came at her the Goddess smashed it to dust with a blow of her fist.

comm.t: The fourth weapon, the śūla, is met with no weapon at all: the Devī shatters it with her fist. Niśumbha is called both asura (9.13) and Dānava here; the epic uses the terms interchangeably for the enemies of the gods.

mantras.anvaya: अथ सः अपि गदाम् आविध्य चण्डिकां प्रति चिक्षेप; सा अपि देव्या त्रिशूलेन भिन्ना भस्मत्वम् आगता।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: the asura’s throw (… चिक्षेप) and the mace’s fate (सा … आगता), with देव्या the agent of भिन्ना.
mantras.lit: Then he too, whirling a mace, hurled it towards Caṇḍikā; it too, split by the Devī with her trident, came to the state of ash.
mantras.tr: Then he whirled a mace and hurled it at Caṇḍikā; but it too, split by the Goddess’s trident, was reduced to ashes.

comm.t: The fifth weapon, the mace, is not merely broken but turned to ash (भस्मत्वम् आगता) by the trident. अपि repeated in both lines marks the rhythm of the sequence: he too threw — it too was destroyed.

mantras.anvaya_en: The absolutive आहत्य (instrument बाणौघैः) precedes the main verb अपातयत; both take the object तम्, qualified by परशुहस्तम्, आयान्तम् and दैत्यपुङ्गवम्.
mantras.lit: Then the Devī, striking him, the bull of the Daityas, coming on with axe in hand, with floods of arrows, felled him to the ground.
mantras.tr: Then, as the chief of the Daityas came on, axe in hand, the Goddess struck him with volleys of arrows and brought him down to the ground.

comm.t: The last weapon of the sequence, the battle-axe, never reaches her: the Devī strikes Niśumbha down with arrows. He falls, but is not yet dead; he rises again in 9.29.

mantras.anvaya: तस्मिन् भीमविक्रमे निशुम्भे भ्रातरि भूमौ निपतिते, (शुम्भः) अतीव संक्रुद्धः अम्बिकां हन्तुं प्रययौ।
mantras.anvaya_en: A long locative absolute (तस्मिन् … भ्रातरि) sets the time; the main clause has an unstated subject, Śumbha, implied by ‘his brother’.
mantras.lit: He, Niśumbha of terrible prowess, the brother, having fallen on the ground, (Śumbha,) exceedingly enraged, set out to kill Ambikā.
mantras.tr: When Niśumbha of terrible might, his brother, had fallen to the ground, Śumbha, wild with rage, set out to kill Ambikā.
mantras.tr_note: Śumbha’s name is supplied; the Sanskrit identifies him only as the fallen hero’s brother.

comm.t: With Niśumbha down, Śumbha takes his place. The verse never names him: he is defined by the brother he has lost, and the sense of the locative भ्रातरि carries the cause of his rage.
Ambikā, ‘Mother’, is the Devī’s name in the most intimate register of the text, even here in battle. Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has it too (295, अम्बिका); the two works remain separate.

mantras.anvaya: सः रथस्थः तथा अत्युच्चैः गृहीतपरमायुधैः अतुलैः अष्टाभिः भुजैः अशेषं नभः व्याप्य बभौ।
mantras.anvaya_en: The main verb बभौ has its subject सः; the absolutive व्याप्य, with the instrumental भुजैः and its qualifiers, says how he shone. अत्युच्चैः may also go with बभौ (‘shone towering high’).
mantras.lit: He, standing in his chariot, and with eight matchless arms holding supreme weapons very high, shone, pervading the entire sky.
mantras.tr: Standing in his chariot, his eight matchless arms raised high, gripping mighty weapons, Śumbha blazed, filling the whole sky.
mantras.tr_note: Śumbha’s name replaces the pronoun सः.

comm.t: Śumbha enters as a towering, eight-armed warrior who seems to fill the sky. The image matches the Devī’s own many arms and weapons, set against her as their rival.

The same compound, गृहीतपरमायुधा, is used of the Devī herself in the Nārāyaṇī hymn (11.16, of Vaiṣṇavī: शङ्खचक्रगदाशार्ङ्गगृहीतपरमायुधे). Here the asura is described in the words the hymn will use for the Goddess.

flags.uncertain: अत्युच्चैः is construed here with गृहीत- (weapons held high); it may equally qualify बभौ or describe Śumbha’s towering size.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two main verbs with one subject (देवी): अवादयत् (object शङ्खम्) and चकार (object ज्याशब्दम्), joined by च अपि.
mantras.lit: Seeing him coming on, the Devī blew her conch, and also made the twang of her bow’s string, exceedingly unbearable.
mantras.tr: Seeing him advance, the Goddess blew her conch and drew from her bowstring a twang that was all but unbearable.

comm.t: The Devī answers Śumbha’s show of arms with sound: the conch and the bowstring. A sequence of sounds follows — her bell (9.20), the lion’s roar (9.21), Kālī’s blow on the earth, which drowns all the earlier sounds (9.22), and Śivadūtī’s laughter (9.23).
The same pattern of sounds — bowstring, lion’s roar, bell, Kālī’s roar — opened the battle in chapter 8 (8.8–10). The conch was the gift of Varuṇa (2.21).

mantras.anvaya: (देवी) समस्तदैत्यसैन्यानां तेजोवधविधायिना निजघण्टास्वनेन च ककुभः पूरयामास।
mantras.anvaya_en: The subject (the Devī) carries over from 9.19. The verb पूरयामास has ककुभः as object and निजघण्टास्वनेन as instrument; the long qualifier with its genitive says what the bell’s sound does.
mantras.lit: And with the sound of her own bell, which brought about the destruction of the vigour of all the Daitya armies, she filled the quarters.
mantras.tr: And she filled every quarter of the sky with the ringing of her bell, a sound that drained the strength of all the Daitya hosts.

comm.t: The bell is the third of the Devī’s sounds. Its power is named exactly: it destroys the तेजस् — the fire, vigour or spirit — of the enemy armies.

The text says the same of the bell elsewhere: it was Indra’s gift, taken from Airāvata (2.22); its sound stupefies the asuras (2.56); and in the Nārāyaṇī hymn the devotee prays to the bell that ‘destroys the tejas of the Daityas’ (हिनस्ति दैत्यतेजांसि, 11.27). In pūjā generally the bell is rung to welcome the gods and keep hostile beings away; these verses are the Devī Māhātmya’s own form of that idea.

samasa.sense: roars that broke the frenzy of the war-elephants
samasa.alt: Also analysable as त्याजिताः इभाः महामदं यैः ते, ‘by which the elephants were made to give up their great rut’; with a causative both persons and things can be its objects, and the sense is the same.

mantras.anvaya: ततः सिंहः त्याजितेभमहामदैः महानादैः गगनं गां तथा एव दश दिशः पूरयामास।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject सिंहः, instrument महानादैः with its qualifier, verb पूरयामास, and three objects: गगनम्, गाम्, दश दिशः.
mantras.lit: Then the lion, with great roars which made the elephants give up their great rut, filled the sky, the earth and likewise the ten directions.
mantras.tr: Then the lion filled the sky, the earth and all ten directions with thunderous roars that broke the frenzy of the war-elephants.

comm.t: The Devī’s lion adds its roar to her sounds. Elephants in rut (मद) are at their most dangerous; the lion’s roar makes them lose it — a conventional image of the lion as the elephant’s master, here aimed at the asura war-elephants.
The ‘ten directions’ are the eight points of the compass with the zenith and the nadir: the roar fills all of space.

mantras.anvaya: ततः काली समुत्पत्य कराभ्यां गगनं क्ष्माम् (च) अताडयत्; तन्निनादेन ते प्राक् स्वनाः तिरोहिताः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences. Kālī’s action (… अताडयत्), with two objects in asyndeton, as गगनं गाम् in 9.21; then the effect (ते … तिरोहिताः), with तन्निनादेन as cause.
mantras.lit: Then Kālī, leaping up, struck the sky and the earth with her two hands; by the din of that, those earlier sounds were drowned out.
mantras.tr: Then Kālī leapt up and struck the sky and the earth with both her hands, and the crash of it drowned every sound that had gone before.

comm.t: Kālī — the fierce form who sprang from the Devī’s brow (7.6) and drank Raktabīja’s blood (8.57–60) — makes the loudest sound of all, and the conch, bowstring, bell and lion’s roar (9.19–21) are lost in it. The Devī named her Cāmuṇḍā for bringing her Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa (7.27), and chapter 8 uses both names of her.

flags.uncertain: गगनम् is taken as a second object of अताडयत् (‘struck the sky and the earth’), in parallel with गगनं गाम् in 9.21. It can also be the goal of समुत्पत्य (‘leaping up into the sky, she struck the earth’).

mantras.anvaya: शिवदूती अशिवम् अट्टाट्टहासं चकार ह। तैः शब्दैः असुराः त्रेसुः, शुम्भः परं कोपं ययौ।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three clauses: Śivadūtī’s laughter (object अट्टाट्टहासम्, verb चकार), its effect on the asuras (instrument तैः शब्दैः, verb त्रेसुः), and on Śumbha (कोपं परं ययौ).
mantras.lit: Śivadūtī let out an ominous peal of loud laughter. By those sounds the asuras trembled; Śumbha went into extreme anger.
mantras.tr: Śivadūtī broke into a terrible, rolling laughter. At that sound the asuras shook with fear, and Śumbha flew into a towering rage.

comm.t: The last of the great sounds of the battle (9.19–23): the Goddess’s conch, bowstring and bell, the lion’s roar, Kālī’s blow on the earth, and now Śivadūtī’s laughter. Sound is a weapon here: it breaks the asuras’ nerve before any blow.
Śivadūtī is the Śakti that came out of Caṇḍikā’s own body in 8.23 and sent Śiva to Śumbha and Niśumbha as her envoy; 8.28 gives the name. Her laughter already felled asuras in 8.38 (चण्डाट्टहासैः).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same name, शिवदूती (name 405). The shared name points to a shared Śākta memory of this episode; the two texts remain distinct works.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) दुरात्मन्, तिष्ठ तिष्ठ इति अम्बिका यदा व्याजहार, तदा आकाशसंस्थितैः देवैः जय इति अभिहितम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A correlative sentence: यदा … व्याजहार (when Ambikā spoke) and तदा … अभिहितम् (then the gods cried). Each clause quotes a cry closed by इति; the second is an impersonal passive with its agent in the instrumental.
mantras.lit: When Ambikā called out, ‘O evil-souled one, stop, stop!’, then ‘Victory!’ was cried by the gods standing in the sky.
mantras.tr: When Ambikā cried, ‘Stand, you wicked one, stand!’, the gods watching from the sky called out, ‘Victory!’
mantras.tr_note: The impersonal passive (‘was cried by the gods’) is turned into an active verb.

comm.t: The Goddess challenges Śumbha in the words the asuras themselves use in battle (तिष्ठ तिष्ठ, as in 2.64), and the gods answer her with the cry जय. Heaven and the battlefield speak at the same moment.
The gods in this carita are onlookers who invoked her (5.9 onward) and cannot fight; their part is to praise. Their cry anticipates the full hymn they will sing in chapter 11 once Śumbha is dead.

Feminine present participle of आ + √या (adādi). For roots of this class in ā the feminine may be formed with or without the nasal (यान्ती / याती); the text has आयान्ती.
Past passive participle of निर् + √अस् ‘to throw’: ‘thrown out, cast off’, here ‘repelled’. It is the main verb of the sentence.

mantras.anvaya: शुम्भेन आगत्य या ज्वालातिभीषणा शक्तिः मुक्ता, सा वह्निकूटाभा आयान्ती (देव्या) महोल्कया निरस्ता।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (या शक्तिः … मुक्ता) names the dart; the main clause (सा … निरस्ता) says what became of it. Both verbs are passive participles; the one who repelled it is not named.
mantras.lit: The dart which, having come up, was released by Śumbha, exceedingly terrible with flames — that (dart), approaching, shining like a heap of fire, was repelled by a great firebrand.
mantras.tr: Śumbha came on and hurled a dart wreathed in dreadful flames. As it came, blazing like a mountain of fire, it was struck aside by a great firebrand.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Mountain of fire’ renders वह्निकूट, literally ‘a heap (or peak) of fire’.

comm.t: Śumbha’s first attack in this round: a burning śakti. The verse does not say who threw the great firebrand (महोल्का) that turned it aside; the context makes it the Goddess, who answers every weapon in these verses.
A śakti hurled at the Goddess is met and undone, as Niśumbha’s was in 9.13. The pattern of the whole battle is that nothing aimed at her reaches her.

flags.uncertain: The agent of निरस्ता is unexpressed; supplying the Goddess (देव्या) follows the context, not the words. महोल्का may be a weapon of hers or a meteor-like missile; the text does not say which.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) अवनीपते, शुम्भस्य सिंहनादेन लोकत्रयान्तरं व्याप्तम्; घोरः निर्घातनिःस्वनः (तं) जितवान्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: a passive one (लोकत्रयान्तरं व्याप्तम्, with the instrument सिंहनादेन) and an active one (निर्घातनिःस्वनः जितवान्) whose object is supplied from the first.
mantras.lit: By the lion-roar of Śumbha the interior of the three worlds was pervaded; a terrible thunderclap-sound overcame (it), O lord of the earth.
mantras.tr: Śumbha’s lion-like roar filled the whole expanse of the three worlds; but a dreadful crash like thunder drowned it, O king.
mantras.tr_note: ‘It’ and ‘but’ are supplied: जितवान् has no expressed object.

comm.t: Śumbha answers the Goddess’s challenge with a roar of his own, and is outmatched even in sound. Medhas turns to his listener (अवनीपते), King Suratha, as he does at moments of tension. Whose thunder it was is not said. Read with 9.19–23, where every sound of the Goddess’s side overwhelms the asuras, the crash is naturally hers; it could also be the crash of the firebrand of 9.25. The text leaves it open.

flags.uncertain: The source of the thunderclap (निर्घातनिःस्वनः) is unstated, and so is the object of जितवान्; the reading ‘overcame Śumbha’s roar’ follows the context.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two parallel clauses share one verb (चिच्छेद) and one instrument (स्वशरैः उग्रैः): the Goddess cut Śumbha’s arrows, and Śumbha cut hers.
mantras.lit: The Goddess (cut) the arrows released by Śumbha, (and) Śumbha the arrows sent by her; they cut them with their own fierce arrows, by hundreds and then by thousands.
mantras.tr: The Goddess cut down the arrows Śumbha loosed, and Śumbha the arrows she sent, each with fierce arrows of their own, by hundreds and by thousands.
mantras.tr_note: The singular चिच्छेद is rendered once for both clauses, with ‘each’ supplied for स्व-.

comm.t: An archery duel in which the two sides cancel each other’s arrows in mid-air. For one verse Śumbha holds his own; the next verse ends it.
A modern reading: the evenly matched exchange shows how long a struggle can seem balanced — and how quickly it turns once the decisive blow comes.

mantras.lit: Then that Caṇḍikā, enraged, struck him with her spear. Struck then, he fell senseless on the ground.
mantras.tr: Then Caṇḍikā in her anger struck him with her spear, and Śumbha, struck down, fell senseless to the earth.

comm.t: Śumbha is struck down and swoons. The verse says मूर्च्छितः, ‘fainted’: he is out of the fight for now, which is why Niśumbha, who had himself been felled in 9.16, rises again in the next verse.
The narrative is careful with the two brothers: Niśumbha’s death comes first, in this chapter; Śumbha’s is kept for chapter 10, after the Goddess has drawn all her Śaktis back into herself.

mantras.lit: Then Niśumbha, having regained consciousness, bow taken up, struck with arrows the Goddess, Kālī and the lion as well.
mantras.tr: Then Niśumbha came to his senses, seized his bow, and shot his arrows at the Goddess, at Kālī, and at the lion.

comm.t: Niśumbha, felled by the Goddess’s arrows in 9.16, recovers and returns to the fight while his brother lies stunned. He aims at all three: the Goddess, Kālī and the lion.
The lion is named here by an epithet, केसरिन् ‘the maned one’. It fights throughout as a warrior in its own right (9.21, 9.37).

mantras.lit: And again the lord of the Dānavas, the son of Diti, having made ten thousand arms, covered Caṇḍikā with discus-weapons.
mantras.tr: Again the Dānava lord took on ten thousand arms, and the son of Diti buried Caṇḍikā under a hail of discuses.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Took on’ renders कृत्वा, ‘having made’; ‘a hail of’ renders the collective singular चक्रायुधेन.

comm.t: Niśumbha’s second assault: he multiplies his arms to ten thousand and hurls discuses from all of them at once. Śumbha had shown eight arms in 9.18; the brothers’ powers of self-multiplication answer the Goddess’s many arms.
दनुज (son of Danu) and दितिज (son of Diti) are used interchangeably of the asuras in the text; both name Niśumbha here.

mantras.anvaya: ततः क्रुद्धा भगवती दुर्गार्तिनाशिनी दुर्गा स्वशरैः तानि चक्राणि तान् सायकान् च चिच्छेद।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject दुर्गा with three epithets; verb चिच्छेद with two objects (तानि चक्राणि, सायकान् तान्) joined by च, and the instrument स्वशरैः.
mantras.lit: Then the Blessed One, enraged — Durgā, destroyer of distress in hard straits — cut with her own arrows those discuses and those arrows.
mantras.tr: Then the blessed Durgā, who ends all distress in hard places, in her anger cut those discuses to pieces with her arrows, and his arrows too.

comm.t: The ten thousand discuses are cut down as easily as single arrows were. The Goddess is named here Durgā with an epithet that explains the name: she destroys the distress (आर्ति) of the hard place (दुर्ग).

The text tells the origin of the name Durgā in her own prophecy (11.49–50, the slaying of the asura Durgama); here the name is glossed by its other traditional sense, the one who rescues from difficulty.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the name दुर्गा (190), followed directly by दुःखहन्त्री (191), ‘destroyer of sorrow’ — the same pairing of name and gloss as in this verse.

mantras.lit: Then Niśumbha, surrounded by the army of the daityas, taking up a mace, indeed rushed swiftly to kill Caṇḍikā.
mantras.tr: Then Niśumbha seized a mace and, with the daitya army all around him, charged at Caṇḍikā to kill her.

comm.t: Niśumbha’s third assault: having lost his bow-and-discus attack, he takes a mace and charges in person with his army about him.
Niśumbha had already thrown a mace at the Goddess in 9.15, and her trident burnt it to ash. Each weapon he takes up is answered and undone; this time she will not wait for it to be thrown.

mantras.tr: Before he could reach her, Caṇḍikā’s keen sword had cut through his mace; and he snatched up a spear.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Before he could reach her’ renders the participle with एव, ‘even while rushing on’.

comm.t: The mace is destroyed before it can be used. Niśumbha changes weapons once more; the spear he now takes is the weapon of his last charge.

mantras.lit: Caṇḍikā pierced in the heart Niśumbha, the tormentor of the immortals, as he came on spear in hand, with a spear hurled with force.
mantras.tr: As Niśumbha, scourge of the gods, came at her spear in hand, Caṇḍikā drove her spear with all her force into his heart.

comm.t: The decisive blow: spear against spear, and hers reaches his heart first. शूल, ‘spear’ or ‘trident’, is the Goddess’s own weapon in this battle (9.15, 9.28).
The epithet अमरार्दन, ‘tormentor of the immortals’, is placed at the moment of his fall: the cause of the gods’ suffering since chapter 5 is now ended by her hand.

mantras.anvaya_en: No finite verb: the participle निःसृतः is the predicate. Subject पुरुषः with अपरः, महाबलः, महावीर्यः and वदन्; source हृदयात् with the genitive phrase भिन्नस्य तस्य शूलेन.
mantras.lit: From the heart of him, pierced by the spear, came forth another being, of great strength, of great valour, saying ‘Stop!’
mantras.tr: Out of his pierced heart came another being, mighty and valiant, crying, ‘Stop!’

comm.t: A strange moment: from Niśumbha’s pierced heart a second figure (अपरः पुरुषः) emerges, still defiant, and shouts the battle-cry ‘Stop!’ that the Goddess had used against Śumbha (9.24). The text does not explain who or what he is.

One traditional reading takes the figure as Niśumbha’s own life or inner strength leaving the body, still bent on battle; the Goddess must cut that down too before he is truly dead. The verse itself says only ‘another man, of great strength’.
A modern reading: what drove Niśumbha does not die with the first wound. It must be met where it comes out of the heart.

flags.uncertain: The identity of the अपरः पुरुषः is not stated; the reading as Niśumbha’s inner self is interpretation, offered as such.

mantras.anvaya: ततः देवी स्वनवत् प्रहस्य निष्क्रामतः तस्य शिरः खड्गेन चिच्छेद। ततः असौ भुवि अपतत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: First sentence: subject देवी, absolutive phrase स्वनवत् प्रहस्य, object शिरः with the genitive तस्य निष्क्रामतः, instrument खड्गेन, verb चिच्छेद. Second: असौ भुवि अपतत्.
mantras.lit: Then the Goddess, laughing aloud, cut off with her sword the head of him who was coming out; thereupon he fell to the ground.
mantras.tr: Then the Goddess laughed aloud and with her sword struck off the head of the one who was coming forth, and he fell to the earth.

comm.t: The Goddess beheads the figure that came out of Niśumbha’s heart, laughing as she does it, and ‘he’ falls. This is the death of Niśumbha that gives the chapter its name (निशुम्भवधः); in 10.2 Śumbha sees his brother slain.

The scene echoes the death of Mahiṣa (3.41–42), struck down by the Goddess’s sword while half-emerged from his own mouth: in both, the asura’s last form is cut down as it comes out. Her laughter (प्रहस्य), as before Mahiṣa’s end (3.34), shows a Goddess untroubled by the fight.

flags.uncertain: असौ (‘he’) may refer to the emerging figure or to Niśumbha; the two are not distinguished by the text, and 10.2 treats Niśumbha as slain.

mantras.anvaya: ततः सिंहः दंष्ट्राक्षुण्णशिरोधरान् तान् असुरान् उग्रं चखाद। तथा काली (चखाद), तथा शिवदूती अपरान् (चखाद)।
mantras.anvaya_en: One verb (चखाद) with the lion as its expressed subject; Kālī and Śivadūtī are added with तथा, and अपरान् gives them their own victims.
mantras.lit: Then the lion fiercely devoured those asuras whose necks were crushed by its fangs; likewise Kālī, likewise Śivadūtī (devoured) others.
mantras.tr: Then the lion savagely devoured the asuras, crushing their necks in its jaws, and Kālī and Śivadūtī devoured others in the same way.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Crushing their necks in its jaws’ renders the compound adjective as an action.

comm.t: With Niśumbha dead, the rout of his army begins. The lion, Kālī and Śivadūtī devour the asuras — the three who are named together again in 9.41.

Kālī and Śivadūtī devour asuras elsewhere in the uttama carita too — Kālī in 7.9–13 and, as Cāmuṇḍā, in the Raktabīja battle (8.53–60); Śivadūtī in 8.38. Devouring is their particular way of ending the enemy.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: केचित् … नेशुः (with a participial compound giving the cause), and अन्ये … निराकृताः (passive, with the instrument तोयेन).
mantras.lit: Some great asuras, pierced by Kaumārī’s spear, perished; others were driven off by water purified by Brahmāṇī’s mantras.
mantras.tr: Some of the great asuras perished, pierced by Kaumārī’s spear; others were routed by water hallowed with Brahmāṇī’s mantras.

comm.t: The Mothers (Mātṛs) who came out of the gods in 8.12–21 join the slaughter, each with the weapon she brought: Kaumārī the spear (8.17), Brahmāṇī the water of her kamaṇḍalu (8.15, 8.33).

The word शक्ति means both the spear Kaumārī carries and the ‘power’ she herself is (the Mothers are the gods’ शक्तयः, 8.13; देवशक्तिभिः, 8.22). The verse uses it in the first sense, but the two are never far apart in this chapter.

mantras.lit: Likewise others, pierced by Māheśvarī’s trident, fell; some were made into powder on the ground by the blows of Vārāhī’s snout.
mantras.tr: Others fell, run through by Māheśvarī’s trident; and some the blows of Vārāhī’s snout ground to dust upon the earth.

comm.t: Two more Mothers act with their own emblems: Māheśvarī, who came on her bull with the trident (8.16), and Vārāhī, who took the form of Viṣṇu’s boar (8.19), using her snout as the boar does.

morph.note: Instrumental singular of वैष्णवी: ī → y before the ending -आ. As the agent of the passive कृताः: ‘(made) by Vaiṣṇavī’. The genitive वैष्णव्याः, ‘(with the discus) of Vaiṣṇavī’, would be printed the same way here (-āḥ loses its visarga before the voiced d) and is equally possible; the instrumental is chosen as the natural agent of कृताः.
Repetition (āmreḍita) of a word expresses distribution or thoroughness: खण्डं खण्डं कृताः ‘made piece by piece’, i.e. hacked to pieces.

mantras.anvaya: वैष्णव्या चक्रेण दानवाः खण्डं खण्डं कृताः, तथा अपरे च ऐन्द्रीहस्ताग्रविमुक्तेन वज्रेण (खण्डं खण्डं कृताः)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A passive sentence (दानवाः … कृताः, agent वैष्णव्या, instrument चक्रेण, predicate खण्डं खण्डम्) and a second that borrows its predicate (अपरे … वज्रेण).
mantras.lit: And the Dānavas were made piece by piece by Vaiṣṇavī with the discus; and likewise others with the thunderbolt released from the tip of Aindrī’s hand.
mantras.tr: Vaiṣṇavī’s discus hacked the Dānavas to pieces, and others in the same way were cut down by the thunderbolt that flew from Aindrī’s hand.
mantras.tr_note: The translation turns the agent and instrument (‘by Vaiṣṇavī with the discus’) into ‘Vaiṣṇavī’s discus’.

comm.t: Vaiṣṇavī with Viṣṇu’s discus (8.18) and Aindrī with Indra’s thunderbolt (8.21) complete the list of the Mothers in action. Nārasiṃhī, who came in 8.20, is not named in these verses.
Each Mother fights with her god’s own weapon: the powers of the gods, who could not win this war themselves, win it as forms of the Goddess. In 10.5–6 she takes them all back into herself.

flags.uncertain: वैष्णव्या (instrumental, ‘by Vaiṣṇavī’) and वैष्णव्याः (genitive, ‘of Vaiṣṇavī’) give the same printed text before दानवाः; the padaccheda follows the instrumental.

morph.note: Perfect 3rd plural of वि + √नश् with e and no reduplication, as नेशुः in 9.38. वि- strengthens the sense: ‘perished utterly’.
Past participle of √नश् (श् + त → ष्ट). Beside विनेशुः ‘perished’ it has its other sense, ‘were lost, vanished’: these asuras fled from the field.
Past passive participle of √भक्ष् (curādi) with the connecting vowel इ: भक्षित ‘eaten’.

mantras.anvaya: केचित् असुराः विनेशुः, केचित् महाहवात् नष्टाः, अपरे च कालीशिवदूतीमृगाधिपैः भक्षिताः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three clauses, each with its own subject (केचित् … केचित् … अपरे): one finite verb (विनेशुः) and two participial predicates (नष्टाः, भक्षिताः).
mantras.lit: Some asuras perished; some vanished from the great battle; and others were devoured by Kālī, Śivadūtī and the lord of beasts.
mantras.tr: Some of the asuras perished, some fled from the great battle, and others were devoured by Kālī, Śivadūtī and the lion.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Fled’ renders नष्टाः, literally ‘were lost (to the battle)’; set against विनेशुः ‘perished’, it means they escaped.

comm.t: The closing verse of the chapter sums up the rout: death, flight, and the devouring by Kālī, Śivadūtī and the lion. Śumbha alone remains, lying stunned (9.28), for the final battle of chapter 10.

The Gita Press pāṭha closes the ninth chapter here, with the colophon that names it निशुम्भवधः, ‘the slaying of Niśumbha’; its 41 mantras include the two uvāca lines. Chapter 10 opens with Śumbha seeing his brother dead and his army being cut down (10.2).
